g r a p h i c a l a b s t r a c t
HE-Cu electrode was fabricated by in situ electrochemical derivation from HKUST-1. The Cu2þ in HKUST-1 was converted to Cu0 nanosheets composed of nanoparticles. HE-Cu exhibited high electrochemical stability and high CO2 adsorption capability. The conversion of CO2 to CO, HCOOH and C2 products was boosted with HE-Cu. Stepped Cu (211) surfaces, (200) facets and Cu edge atoms were active sites.

Handling Editor: E. Brillas
Keywords: Cu electrode MOF derivation Electrochemical CO2 reduction C2 product selectivity
a b s t r a c t
A novel electrode composed of Cu nanosheets constructed from nanoparticles was synthesized by in situ electrochemical derivation from the metal-organic framework (MOF) HKUST-1. The prepared derivative electrode (HE-Cu) exhibited higher Faradaic efficiency (FE, 56.0%) of electrochemical CO2 reduction (CO2R) compared with that of pristine Cu foil (p-Cu, 32.3%) at an overpotential of 1.03 V vs. a reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE). HE-Cu also exhibited lower onset potential of CO2R as well as inhibiting the H2 evolution reaction. Electrochemical measurements revealed that HE-Cu exhibited higher CO2 adsorption (1.58-fold) and a larger electrochemical active surface area (1.24-fold) compared with p-Cu. Physicochemical characterization and Tafel analysis showed that stepped Cu (211) surfaces, (200) facets and Cu edge atoms on HE-Cu contributed significantly to the enhanced CO2R activity and/or HCOOH and/or C2 product selectivity. The FEs of HCOOH and C2 products for HE-Cu increased 1.57-fold and 10.6-fold at an overpotential of 1.19 V vs. RHE compared with p-Cu. Although CH4 was produced on p-Cu, its formation was totally suppressed on HE-Cu due to the increase of edge sites and (200) facets. Our study demonstrates that electroreduction of MOFs is a promising method to prepare novel and stable electrochemical
catalysts with unique surface structures. The fabricated derivative electrode not only promoted electrochemical CO2R activity but also exhibited high C2 product selectivity.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Conversion of CO2 into economically valuable chemicals and fuels can not only help to mitigate global warming but also contribute to addressing the energy crisis. Various technological routes, such as electrocatalytic (Gattrell et al., 2006; Liu et al., 2020), photocatalytic reduction (Shehzad et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2020), chemical and biochemical reduction (Appel et al., 2013) have been employed for the reduction of CO2 to reusable hydrocarbons (Shao et al., 2020). Among them, electrochemical CO2 reduction (CO2R) is believed to have advantages that include mild reaction conditions, controllable product selectivity and easy scalability (Gattrell et al., 2007; Kondratenko et al., 2013; Oloman and Li, 2008). Moreover, the method is attractive for solving energy and environmental problems because electricity can be generated using renewable sources, including solar andwind. Nonetheless, the electrochemical CO2R is thermodynamically difficult, demanding ca. 220e330 kJ mol 1 of energy to break the C]O bond (Qiu et al., 2016). To address this challenge, an electrocatalytic electrode with excellent performance is required to overcome the activation energy barrier.
Recently, various sp metals, d metals and their complexes have been explored for diverse electrocatalytic applications of CO2R. Most electrocatalysts produce CO and formic acid (HCOOH) as the major products (Hori, 2008; Teeter and Van Rysselberghe, 1954). In contrast, the electronic configuration of Cu enables catalytic reduction of CO2 tomore reduced species such as hydrocarbons and alcohols. Furthermore, Cu catalysts allow the formation of C1eC3 products via CO2 electroreduction (Hori, 2008; Kuhl et al., 2012). This feature is highly desirable because the synthesis of longcarbon-chain products is complex and energy-demanding. However, CO2 electroreduction on Cu electrodes requires ca. 1 V of overpotential, causing considerable energy losses (Kuhl et al., 2012). The catalytic activity of an electrode depends on characteristics such as morphology, composition, crystal structure, surface area and particle size (Anggraini et al., 2013; Brouzgou et al., 2014). Of these factors, surface morphology has been demonstrated to influence catalytic activity of Cu towards electrochemical CO2R. This is because the morphology influences the density of undercoordinated sites, which serve as the active sites for CO2R (Tang et al., 2012). It has been demonstrated that a decrease of catalyst size can lead to an increase in the number of undercoordinated sites (Mistry et al., 2014). Hence, the development of Cu catalysts with smaller particle size is highly desirable. Selectivity for CO2R products is also significantly dependent on the surface structure, morphology and coordinated surface sites (such as steps, corner and apex sites or crystal boundaries) of Cu catalysts (Simon et al., 2021). Roberts et al. fabricated a novel Cu nanocube electrocatalyst that exhibited high selectivity for ethylene formation from CO2R (Roberts et al., 2015).
On the other hand, the activities of electrocatalysts often suffer from sluggish kinetics. The poor solubility of CO2 in water means that its capture, a prerequisite for highly efficient CO2R, is usually limited (Liu et al., 2013). To achieve efficient CO2 electroreduction, enhancement of CO2 adsorption onto the electrode surface has been recognized as an effective strategy. Thus, a broad range of research efforts have been devoted to improving CO2 adsorption on
electrocatalytic electrodes, such as creating oxygen vacancies, doping with chemical elements and coupling chemicals, in an attempt to lower the overpotential, boost the reaction kinetics and increase product selectivity (Chen et al., 2020). Despite the great progress made in the improvement of CO2 adsorption, it is still necessary to exploit other materials to enrich the concentration of CO2 on the electrode surface.
Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) are inorganic-organic hybrid crystalline compounds that have well-defined structures and permanent porosity. MOFs have several advantageous features, such as high surface areas, controllable porous structures and high-density coordination-unsaturated metal sites (Li et al., 2018). Chui et al. (1999) reported a MOF named HKUST-1 (Cu3(BTC)2, BTC ¼ 1,3,5- benzenetricarboxylic acid) consisting of highly dispersed copper oxide nodes and organic ligands, which has received much attention in recent decades owing to its high surface area and large pore volume. Furthermore, Chen et al. (2018) reported that the HKUST-1 they prepared exhibited high CO2 uptake of 4.2 mmol g 1 at 1 bar and 27 C. Based on this result, we suggest that HKUST-1 could be considered as a potential copper-based cathode for electroreduction of CO2. However, our preliminary experiment showed that HKUST-1 grown on copper foam rapidly became unstable during electrolysis. Huang et al. (2021) also reported this phenomenon and they fabricated a MOF-derived porous copper oxide carbon (CuOx-C) electrode by calcinating the Cu-MOF. Interestingly, we happened on the unexpected discovery that the organic ligands in HKUST-1 were completely removed and elemental copper was deposited from copper oxide nodes after electroreduction. The obtained copper derivative (HE-Cu) not only had a new sheet-like morphology, but was also electrocatalytically stable in the subsequent CO2R processes. Moreover, HE-Cu achieved higher Faradaic efficiency (FE) for carbonaceous products than pristine copper foam. This surprising discovery provides a new approach for preparing novel metal electrodes with high catalytic activity for potential electrocatalytic applications.
In this study, a novel strategy using a MOF as template coupled with electroreduction to fabricate a copper cathode, HE-Cu, was proposed and validated. The physicochemical and electrochemical properties of HE-Cu were characterized by various analytical techniques. The activity and selectivity of HE-Cu during electrochemical CO2R to C1 and C2 products under different electrolytic potentials were evaluated in-depth. The reaction mechanisms for CO2R and product generation on the surface of HE-Cu were also considered.

sections.heading: 2.1. Reagents and materials
sections.text:
All chemicals were of reagent grade and were used without further purification. Ethanol (CH3CH2OH), acetone (CH3COCH3), HCOOH, ammonium persulfate ((NH4)2S2O8), potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3), H3BTC, sodium hydroxide (NaOH) and concentrated sulfuric acid 98.0% (H2SO4) were purchased from Aladdin Reagent Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Ultra-high purity nitrogen (N2, purity 99.99%), hydrogen (H2, purity 99.999%), air (highly purified), argon (Ar, purity 99.99%), CO2 (purity 99.995%) and carbonmonoxide (CO,
purity 99.99%) were supplied by Hangzhou Jing Gong Special Gas Co., Ltd. (Hangzhou, China). Calibration gases containing 1000 ppm ofmethane (CH4), ethane (C2H6) and ethene (C2H4) were purchased from Dalian Special Gases Co., Ltd. (Dalian, China). Copper foam (purity 99.9%) used as the electrode substrate was provided by Jianhua Protection Material Co., Ltd. (Jinan, China). High purity Milli-Q water (MQ, 18.2 MU cm) produced from a Millipore Milli-Q purification system was used throughout unless specifically stated otherwise.

sections.heading: 2.2.1. In situ synthesis of Cu(OH)2 on Cu foam
sections.text:
Cu(OH)2 nanotubes were generated in situ on the surface of Cu foam using the alkaline oxidation method reported by Okada et al. (2014). Typically, copper foam (10 mm 20 mm 1.2 mm) was soaked in acetone for 10 min and then washed sequentially with 0.5 M H2SO4 and MQ for 5 min in order to remove the oxide layer and impurities. After drying with N2 gas, the dried clean pristine copper foam (p-Cu) was immersed in a mixture of 10 M NaOH solution (4mL),1M (NH4)2S2O8 solution (4mL) andMQ (7mL), and kept at room temperature for 30 min. After the in situ alkaline oxidation process, copper foam covered with Cu(OH)2 nanotubes (OHeCu) was obtained and then washed with ethanol and MQ for further use. The OHeCu electrode became black after in situ alkaline oxidation, as shown in Fig. SM-1.
2.2.2. In situ fabrication of HKUST-1 on Cu foam from OHeCu The HKUST-1-covered Cu foam electrode was synthesized as follows: OHeCu was soaked in a mixture of MQ (1.8 mL), ethanol (4.67 mL) and H3BTC (0.21 g) for 5 min. During the soaking process, the solution changed from transparent to increasingly blue over time while the color of the electrode changed from black to dark blue (Fig. SM-1), indicating the successful formation of HKUST-1 on Cu foam (HeCu). The HeCu was washed with ethanol and MQ several times and then dried.

sections.text:

The MOF-derived copper electrode was synthesized by simple electrochemical reduction of the HeCu electrode through chronoamperometry at a potential of 1.2 V vs a saturated calomel electrode (SCE) for 30 min in 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte. The resulting electrode was dark bronze in color (shown in Fig. SM-1) and named as HE-Cu (H and E representing HKUST-1 and electroreduction). The processes for the preparation of all electrodes are shown in Fig. SM-2.

sections.heading: 2.3.1. Physicochemical characterization
sections.text: The structural properties of the prepared electrodes were studied by X-ray diffraction (XRD) using a PANalytical X’Pert PRO diffractometer (Malvern Panalytical, UK). This diffractometer emits Cu Ka radiation working at a voltage of 40 kV and current of 40 mA. The surface morphologies of the electrodes were observed by field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) using an S-4800 instrument (Hitachi, Japan) with an accelerating voltage of 5 kV. The crystal structure of copper was determined using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) on a Tecnai G2 F30 S-Twin (Philips-FEI, Netherlands) operated at 300 kV.

sections.heading: 2.3.2. Electrochemical characterization
sections.text:
Electrochemical characterization was conducted using an electrochemical workstation (CHI-660D, CH Instrument, China) and a
three-electrode system. The characterization was performed in an H-type cell separated with a Nafion® 117 membrane. The anolyte and catholyte were 0.5 M NaOH and CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solutions, respectively. The anodic chamber was open to the air. The cathodic chamber was sealed with a sufficiently tight-fitting lid, containing copper foam electrode port, SCE reference electrode port and sampling port, to avoid the loss of gaseous products. HECu or p-Cu (1 cm 2 cm) were used as the working electrode, platinum sheet as the counter electrode, and Ag/AgCl as the reference electrode. The catholyte was stirred continuously with a magnetic stirrer. Roughness factors (RF) were derived from the electrochemical surface areas (ECSA) of the electrodes, obtained from the double-layer capacitance (Cdl). Measurements were made in 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (100 mL) in the range of open potential (±50 mV) in a non-Faradaic current range. The Cdl was calculated according to the relationship between the capacitor current and the scanning rate during double layer charge as shown in Eq. (1)
i ¼ v Cdl (1)
where i is the charging current and v is the scan rate. Plotting i as a function of v yields a straight line with slope equal to Cdl.
The ECSA of the catalyst can be calculated by dividing Cdl by the specific capacitance (Cs, assumed as 20 mF cm 2 in this study) as shown in Eq. (2)
ECSA ¼ Cdl=Cs (2) The RF can be calculated by dividing ECSA by the geometric area of the electrode (2 cm2 in this study). Chronoamperometric measurements (He et al., 2018) were used to determine the response current of CO2 adsorption on the electrode surface. The control voltage was 1.2 V vs Ag/AgCl. In order to exclude the influence of dissolved O2, the cathode solution was CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution (100 mL). The relationship between the electrochemical reaction rates to various overpotentials was described by the Tafel equation for the electrochemical CO2R process (Hasani et al., 2020).

sections.heading: 2.4. Electroreduction of CO2
sections.text:
The three-electrode system and electrochemical workstation employed for electrochemical CO2R were the same as those used for electrochemical characterization. A thermostatic water bath (THD-2015, Ningbo Tianheng Instrument Factory, China) was used to maintain the electrolyte temperature at 25 C. The initial pH of the system is ca. 6.73 and the final pH ranged from 6.8 to 7.5, which did not significantly change. Periodically, gas and aqueous samples were taken using a gas-tight syringe and analyzed by gas chromatography (GC) and ion chromatography (IC). All potentials were calibrated to RHE scale as shown in Eq. (3):
E ¼ E ðvs: SCEÞ þ 0:2412 V þ 0:0591 V pH þ iRu (3)
where E the final reported potential, i is the average current and Ru is the uncompensated solution resistance as determined by potentiostatic electrochemical impedance spectroscopy.

sections.heading: 2.5. Analytical methods
sections.text:
The concentration of H2 and CO in gas phase products was quantitatively analyzed by gas chromatograph (GC, GC-7890B, Agilent, USA), equipped with HP-MOLESIEVE column (30 m 320 mm 12 mm) and TCD detector. Detection conditions: inlet heater 60 C, pressure 10 psi, split mode off, purge flow to split outlet 60 mL min 1, purge time 0.75 min, column constant flow
mode, oven temperature 50 C, Equilibrium time 0.5 min, holding time 10 min, detector 120 C, reference flow rate 10 mL min 1, carrier gas: high purity He (for CO determination) or Ar (for H2 determination), flow rate 2.0 mLmin 1; The gas injection volume is 1 mL.
The concentration of gas product methane was measured by GC (GC-2014, Shimadzu, Japan), equipped with HP-PLOT/Q capillary column (30 m 320 mm 20 mm) and FID detector. Detection conditions: column temperature, 90 C; inlet temperature, 120 C; detector temperature, 200 C; carrier gas: high purity N2, flow rate 2.0 mL min 1; split ratio: 18:1; gas: high purity H2, the flow rate is 50mLmin 1; the supporting gas: air, the flow rate is 160mLmin 1; the makeup gas: high purity N2, the flow rate is 50 mL min 1; the gas injection volume is 1.0 mL.
The formic acid in the liquid phase was measured by ion chromatograph (IC, ICS 2000, Dionex, USA). The IC was equipped with a double piston pump, separated by IonPac AS19 analytical column (4 mm 250 mm, Dionex), and IonPac AS19 guard column (4 mm 250 mm, Dionex), conductivity detector (DS6, Dionex), anion electrolysis suppressor (4 mm ASRS, Dionex) as eluent, pump pressure 2000 psi, column temperature 35 C, suppressor current 100 mA, eluent concentration 20 mol L 1, 10-30-10 min gradient elution mode, liquid injection volume 1 mL.
The catalytic selectivity and activity of theworking electrode are expressed by FE and partial current density (PCD), respectively. FE can be calculated using Eq. (4):
FE ¼ znF=Q (4)
where z is the number of electrons transferred during CO2 reduction to product, n is the number of moles of reaction product (mol), F is the Faraday constant (96,485C mol 1) and Q is the total electric charge input in the reaction process (C).
PCD can be calculated using Eq. (5):
PCD ¼ jtotal FE (5)
where jtotal is total current density.

sections.heading: 3.1. Structure and morphology analysis
sections.text:
The XRD patterns of p-Cu, HeCu and HE-Cu are shown in Fig. 1. As can be seen, the diffraction peaks of HeCu are clearly related to those of simulated HKUST-1 peaks (CCDC 112954) as shown in Fig. 1a, suggesting the successful preparation of HKUST-1 on the
surface of Cu foam (Heinen et al., 2018). The XRD of the HE-Cu electrode synthesized by electroreduction using HeCu as precursor contained diffraction peaks at the same positions as those of pCu (shown in Fig. 1b), corresponding to the standard pattern of copper (JCPDS No. 04e0836). The diffraction peaks at 43.3 , 50.4 and 74.1 shown in Fig. 1b were indexed to (111), (200) and (220) planes of Cu0, confirming that the valence of copper in HE-Cu was reduced to zero after electroreduction. However, the peak intensity ratio of (200) to (111) was significantly enhanced after the HKUST-1 derivation treatment. The (200)/(111) ratio of p-Cu was 0.51, which is close to the standard pattern of copper (0.46), while the (200)/ (111) ratio of HE-Cu was increased to 0.73. These results demonstrated that HE-Cu exposedmore (200) facets than p-Cu. It has been reported that different intensity ratios of crystal planes in metal electrodes such as Cu and Agwould show remarkable differences in CO2 reduction activity and product selectivity during electrochemical CO2R (Ajmal et al., 2020; Ham et al., 2017).
The morphologies and structures of the fabricated electrodes were further investigated by FE-SEM and TEM. The surface morphology of p-Cu was smooth, as shown in Fig. SM-3, while that of OHeCu was composed of 120 nm diameter nanotubes (Fig. 2a). The morphology of OHeCu was consistent with that reported previously (Okada et al., 2014), as a consequence of the oxidizing power of (NH4)2S2O8 in strong alkaline solution. The surface morphology of HKUST-1 on the surface of the HeCu electrode is shown in Fig. 2b. The HKUST-1 was composed of octahedra with average diameters of 200e500 nm, but the edges of the octahedra appeared to be quite coarse. The coarseness may be due to 1): the rapid reaction between Cu(OH)2 and H3BTC (within 5 min); 2): insufficient Cu(OH)2 precursor and fast generation of excess HKUST-1 nuclei; 3): the Cu(OH)2 was already heterogeneous and dispersed non-uniformly on the Cu foam (Wang et al., 2018).
Fortunately, the coarse shape of HKUST-1 did not affect the formation of the HE-Cu electrode (Fig. 2c) where metallic copper nanosheets were formed with an average length of 500 nm and thickness of 120 nm after electroreduction treatment. Unlike the surface of p-Cu, the copper nanosheets on the HE-Cu electrode surface were rough and irregular as shown in Fig. 2d. The enlarged image of the HE-Cu electrode revealed that the surface of the nanosheets was constructed from large numbers of nanoparticle subunits with a diameter of 40e50 nm. This suggests a substantially larger specific surface area and more exposed CO2R active sites such as edge and corner sites. Since a nanosheet has twelve edges and consists of numerous nanoparticles, edge sites can be considered as the extra active sites for CO2R on the surface of HE-Cu compared with p-Cu. We can deduce that the BTC3 ligand

The low magnification FE-SEM images of OHeCu, HeCu and HE-Cu electrodes are shown in Fig. SM-4, demonstrating their uniformity.
The nanosheet-like morphology of the HE-Cu electrode was further confirmed by TEM (Fig. 3a). The joined copper nanosheets formed a net structure that adhered to the Cu foam. The observed lattice spacings of 0.181 and 0.209 nmmatched the (200) and (111) plane of Cu0 as shown in Fig. 3b, consistent with the XRD results. The presence of regular moir e patterns (thick black fringe) in Fig. 3b proved the stacking layer structure of Cu atoms (Pochet et al., 2017).
Interestingly, we found clearly step-like structures on the surface of HE-Cu, which is considered to be Cu (211) surface (Fig. 3c). A perspective view of the model (211) surface of Cu is shown in Fig. 3d. The stepped Cu (211) surface was composed of 4-fold coordination steps and 3-fold coordination terraces in the (111) geometry. As shown in Fig. 3c, the HE-Cu nanosheet consisted of at least 4 layers of Cu nanostructures, resulting in the presence of at

The three red parallelograms reveal the 3 bottom layers and highlight the stepped Cu (211) surfaces. In the region between the red parallelograms and red broken line, the lattice fringe was discontinuous, confirming the presence of stepped structures. Several groups have proved that stepped Cu (211) surfaces greatly enhance hydrocarbon production in electrochemical CO2R (Durand et al., 2011; Roberts et al., 2015; Sen et al., 2014). The enhancement originating from stepped (211) surfaces is mainly attributed to their stronger bonding to hydrocarbon intermediates than Cu (111) and Cu (200) facets. The role of stepped Cu (211) surfaces in this study will be discussed later.

sections.heading: 3.2. Activity and selectivity of electrocatalytic reduction of CO2
sections.text:

The related FEs of each product as a function of time (120 min) for HE-Cu and p-Cu are shown in Fig. SM-5 and Fig. SM-6. Both HE-Cu and p-Cu approached almost 100% total FEs for all products at a wide potential (shown in Fig. 4a). The HE-Cu electrode resulted in significantly less H2 evolution reaction (HER) to CO2R, with more HCOOH and CO production than p-Cu in the range from 0.35 to 1.32 V vs. RHE. The maximum FE selectivities of 40.1% ± 1.7% and 12.1% ± 2.9% for HCOOH and CO were obtained on HE-Cu at 1.03 V. Upon further increasing the overpotential, the FEs of HCOOH and CO decreased while the reaction selectivity shifted to HER because the CO2R activity starts to become mass transport limited on planar electrodes (Kuhl et al., 2012; Tomboc et al., 2020). The production of CO and HCOOH on HE-Cu started at an onset potential of 0.35 V vs. RHE, while the CO2R products were still undetected on p-Cu, showing that HE-Cu was more favorable for CO2R since it exhibited lower onset potential than p-Cu. Fig. 4b shows other CO2R products. C2H4 and C2H6 were found in both HE-Cu and p-Cu while CH4 was only found in pCu. On the HE-Cu electrode, the highest FEs of C2H4 and C2H6 were 2.93% ± 0.6% and 2.58% ± 0.6% at a potential of 1.19 V. Although the FEs never exceeded 5% for any of the overpotentials in this study, the enhanced rates were greater than 9.1- and 13.0-fold compared with those of p-Cu, demonstrating that the HE-Cu electrode has potential to increase the selectivity for C2 products.
Another important property for evaluating the performance of CO2R is the current density that can be reached by changing the potential, as shown in Fig. 4c and d. The concentration of each product as a function of potential and time are plotted in Fig. SM-7 and Fig. SM-8. As shown in Fig. 4c and d, the total current density and PCD of all products increased as the overpotential for both
electrodes decreased. Consistently, HE-Cu exhibited larger PCD values of all products except PCDH2 at all applied potentials compared to those of p-Cu, suggesting that HE-Cu has higher intrinsic activity than p-Cu (Clark et al., 2018). Neither HE-Cu nor pCu exhibited distinct PCD profiles, indicating that discrete potentials did not drive CO2R in this study (Calvinho et al., 2018). Notably, PCDHCOOH and PCDCO of the HE-Cu electrode at 1.03 V were 10.26 ± 0.47 and 3.11 ± 0.76 mA cm 2, while the corresponding values for the p-Cu electrode were 3.90 ± 0.77 and 0.93 ± 0.08 mA cm 2 under the same conditions. These results clearly demonstrated that the HE-Cu electrode exhibited enhanced electrocatalytic activity for CO2R to CO and HCOOH. Fig. 4d plots the PCD of CH4, C2H4 and C2H6 for the HE-Cu and p-Cu electrodes, which had a similar trend to Fig. 4c. The PCDC2H6 and PCDC2H4 of the HE-Cu electrode at 1.19 V were 0.89 ± 0.14 and 1.02 ± 0.26mA cm 2, which were 16.48- and 11.69-fold higher than those of p-Cu. This result is consistent with the results shown in Fig. 4d, indicating that the HE-Cu electrode was more selective for the generation of C2 products. The appearance of the HE-Cu electrode did not change after electrochemical CO2R (shown in Fig. SM1), and the peak intensity of (200) facets of the HE-Cu electrode remained stable after CO2R (shown in Fig. SM-9). The (200)/(111) ratio of HE-Cu electrode was 0.74 after CO2R, which is close to the fresh one (0.73), indicating its stability.

sections.heading: 3.3. Surface electrochemical characterization
sections.text:
The adsorption of CO2 on the electrode surface is critical for electrochemical CO2R. Hence, the HE-Cu and p-Cu electrodes were analyzed by chronoamperometry. Fig. SM-10a shows the j-t (current-time) responses of the HE-Cu and p-Cu electrodes. Since the change of current density (j(t)) with time t is related to the amount
of CO2 adsorbed, according to the Cottrell equation (Eq. (6)) (He et al., 2018), the limit of current density (j∞) is related to CO2 concentration.
jjðtÞj ¼ nF ffiffiffiffiffiffi D0 pt r CCO2 (6)
where n, F, D0, t and CCO2 are the stoichiometric number of electrons involved in the reaction, Faraday’s constant, the diffusion constant, time and the concentration of electroactive species, respectively.
According to the reaction pathway hypothesized by Hori et al. (1986) electrochemical CO2R rate is dependent on the reduction of adsorbed CO2 on the electrode surface. As shown in Fig. SM-10a, the corresponding j∞ on HE-Cu was 25.7 mA cm 2 at 1.2 V vs Ag/ AgCl., about 1.58 times that of the p-Cu electrode, indicating that the HE-Cu electrode surface adsorbed more CO2 and had better CO2R kinetics than the p-Cu electrode.
To further investigate the mechanism for the enhanced CO2R activity of HE-Cu, the electrochemically active surface area (ECSA), roughness factor (RF) and double-layer capacitance (Cdl) of HE-Cu and p-Cu electrodes were measured by cyclic voltammetry (CV), as shown in Fig. SM-11. The RF and Cdl values derived from these curves are provided in Fig. SM-10b and Table 1. As shown in Fig. SM10b, the Cdl of HE-Cu and p-Cu electrodes were 1848 and 1487 mF cm 2 from the slopes of the charge current proportionalpotential scanning rate curves. The RF of the HE-Cu electrode was calculated as 92.4 cm2, which is 1.24 times larger than that of the pCu electrode. This proves that the catalytic performance of the HECu electrode can be partially attributed to the higher ECSA of the nanosheet-like structure.
To gain insights into the charge-transfer kinetics of the CO2 electroreduction reaction, the Tafel plots for HCOOH and CO formation were obtained by plotting the iRu-corrected electrode potentials vs. the logarithms of PCDCO (log(jCO)) and PCDHCOOH (log(jHCOOH)), respectively. As shown in Fig. 5, log(jCO) and log(jHCOOH) increased linearly in the charge-transfer-limited regime for p-
Cu and HE-Cu, implying that CO production and HCOOH formation proceeded via independent pathways. The HE-Cu Tafel slopes of 86.0 and 95.7 mV dec 1 for CO2 reduction to CO and HCOOH, respectively, were lower than those for p-Cu (107.1 and 105.2 mV dec 1).

sections.heading: 3.4. Surface enhanced CO2R mechanism
sections.text:
It is well known that the activity of a catalyst for electrochemical CO2R depends strongly on ECSA, surface active sites (such as edge or apex sites) and exposed crystal facets. In order to explore the effects of other factors on CO2R activity of HE-Cu, PCDCO and PCDHCOOH were normalized with RF values to exclude the influence of ECSA, namely SACO and SAHCOOH. The experimental PCDCO and PCDHCOOH data were selected from the Tafel region ( 0.36 to 0.54 V shown in Fig. 5) and the calculated SACO and SAHCOOH values are listed in Table 1. Briefly, SACO and SAHCOOH were higher for HE-Cu than p-Cu at all three overpotentials. For instance, HE-Cu gave high SACO and SAHCOOH values of 0.66 and 3.13 mA cm 2, which were 5.1- and 5.7-fold higher than those of p-Cu. These results suggest that factors other than ECSA played a key role in the electrochemical CO2R process, probably related to the surface structure of the electrode.
The general scheme for generation of HCOOH and CO on Cu electrodes by electrochemical CO2R is illustrated in Eqs. (7)e(12). Two possible rate-determining steps for CO2 electroreduction have been postulated by other researchers (Chen et al., 2012; Zheng et al., 2018). One suggested that the first electron transfer to CO2 to form CO2 (Eq. (7)), with a Tafel slope of 118 mV dec 1, is the rate determining step. The other proposed that protonation of CO2 (Eq. (8)), with a Tafel slope of 59 mV dec 1, is the rate determining step. In the present work, the Tafel slope for p-Cu was close to 118 mV dec 1, indicating that formation of CO2 by the initial e transfer controlled the total reduction reaction rate. This is because the step requires a more negative potential relative to the subsequent steps. In comparison, HE-Cu gave Tafel slopes of 95.7 and 86.0 mV dec 1
on of CO2 using the HE-Cu (a) and p-Cu (b) electrodes.
for CO2R to HCOOH and CO. The results were similar to those reported by Zheng et al. (2018) who determined that Hþ transfer to CO2 was the rate determining step. Moreover, according to the Tafel slopes derived from first principles, Eq. (8) is also believed to be the rate determining step for electroreduction of CO2 on the HECu electrode. These results not only explain the higher electrochemical CO2R activity of HE-Cu, but also provide a reason for the lower onset potential of HE-Cu for electrochemical CO2R compared to p-Cu.

Where * in the Eqs represents the active sites on the electrode surface.
An ideal electrocatalyst for CO2R should bind CO2R intermediates (i.e., CO* or HCOO*/COOH*) sufficiently strong. In this respect, exposed facets, edge and apex sites on Cu with intrinsically distinct chemical features exhibit different functionalities for adherence of intermediates (Loiudice et al., 2016; Lysgaard et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2013). It has been demonstrated that different crystal facets exhibit distinct reactivities in electrochemical CO2R. Density functional theory (DFT)-calculated results confirmed that the catalyst surfaces stabilized key intermediates in the CO2 electroreduction in the order Cu (211) > Cu (200) > Cu (111) (Durand et al., 2011; Feng et al., 2020). The stepped (211) surfaces of Cu catalysts have been considered as active sites during electrochemical CO2R and favor the formation of HCOOH compared with terrace (111) and (200) facets based on DFT calculations (Sen et al., 2014). It is believed that the binding energy between CO2 and the stepped Cu (211) surface is suitable for the activation of inert O] C]O bonds, leading to the formation of *CO. The generated *CO also binds moderately with the stepped Cu (211) surface allowing further protonation of *CO to *COH/CHO* through Eq. (12), where *COH/CHO* has beenwidely identified as a significant intermediate for C2 product generation through Eqs. (13)e(16) (Montoya et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2018). From the TEM results shown in Fig. 3, the stepped Cu (211) surface was present on the surface of HE-Cu but was not found on p-Cu. Therefore, HE-Cu exhibited higher Faradaic efficiency for HCOOH and higher selectivity for C2 product generation than the p-Cu electrode in the reduction of CO2 in aqueous solution. The influence of the stepped Cu (211) surface on p-Cu is negligible, so the intermediate *CH2O preferentially generates CH4 through Eq. (16).

Size-dependent activity and selectivity of the prepared Cu catalysts should also be considered for electrochemical CO2R. As
shown in the FE-SEM of HE-Cu (Fig. 2), the rough Cu nanosheets consisted of numerous Cu particles with sizes in the range of 40e50 nm, suggesting the presence of more edge sites on the HECu surface. Similar Cu nanocrystals were also mentioned by Loiudice et al. (2016) in their previous work. They fabricated Cu cubes of various sizes and found that the Cu atoms on the edge sites favored the CO2R reaction and inhibited the HER. Edge sites also influence the CO2R selectivity towards CeC coupling, resulting in higher C2 and lower CH4 production. Consequently, higher CO2R activity and C2 product selectivity, combined with HER inhibition, were achieved by the presence of edge sites on the surface of HECu. Although the role of edge sites has been established, there are still large numbers of corner sites present on the HE-Cu surface whose contribution to CO2R activity and selectivity is still unclear and needs further study.
The XRD results (Fig. 1) proved the higher ratio of (200)/(111) on the surface of HE-Cu. The decreased exposure of (111) facets could inhibit production of CH4 (Loiudice et al., 2016), which would explain the suppression of CH4 generation by HE-Cu. Furthermore, (200) facets have been shown to be highly favorable for C2 product formation in electrochemical CO2R, which is also in agreement with our results (Ajmal et al., 2020; Loiudice et al., 2016). Both experimental data and theoretical studies suggest that the rate of reduction of ethylene oxide (C2H4O) to C2H4 is markedly higher on more open (200) facets than on close-packed (111) facets, enhancing the activity and selectivity of HE-Cu to produce C2H4 and C2H6 rather than CH4 (Garza et al., 2018; Hori et al., 2002; Nie et al., 2013: Schouten et al., 2013). The combination of (200) facets with other properties of HE-Cu, such as edge sites, leads to preferential production of C2H4 and C2H6 compared to p-Cu (Liu et al., 2017).
The enhanced mechanisms for HE-Cu catalyzed electrochemical CO2R are summarized in Fig. 6. After electrochemical reduction of the MOF, HKUST-1, the derived HE-Cu exhibited higher CO2 adsorption and larger ESCA. Both of these characteristics enhanced CO2R activity. Furthermore, the derived HE-Cu consisted of nanosheets composed of numerous 40e50 nm nanoparticle subunits. The unique surface properties resulted in more edge sites, stepped Cu (211) surfaces and (200) facets. These surface structures have multi-functional roles in CO2R, mainly influencing activity and selectivity.
As shown in Fig. 6, the presence of edge Cu atoms on the HE-Cu surface, combined with higher CO2 adsorption and larger ESCA, enhanced CO2R activity about 1.73-fold compared with p-Cu at an overpotential of 1.03 V vs. RHE. Not surprisingly, the HER was inhibited on HE-Cu under the same conditions. The stepped Cu (211) surfaces may significantly influence both HCOOH and C2 product selectivity. Since (211) surfaces favor HCOOH formation
compared to terrace (111) and (200) facets, 1.57-fold higher FE for HCOOH generation was obtained with HE-Cu compared to p-Cu. The (211) surface enhanced the selectivity for C2 products during CO2R on HE-Cu through a similar mechanism to that of (200) facets. The enhanced generation of C2 products on HE-Cu is mainly due to the formation, adsorption and stabilization of key intermediates such as CO*, *COH/CHO* and C2H4O on (211) surfaces or (200) facets, leading to a 10.6-fold increase of FEs for total C2 products.
Overall, CO2R is an emerging and promising strategy for converting CO2 into high value-added fuels or chemicals in terms of sustainable chemistry. But its practical implementations were still problematic due to its low conversion rate, poor selectivity for high-value products or uncertain stability. Baes on the existing research, copper-based electrode is still the first choice for the production of C2 products at present during the CO2R. Therefore, the HE-Cu electrode prepared in this study successfully improved the CO2R activity and C2 products selectivity. Also, the in situ MOF derivation method provide a new idea to fabricate novel metalbased electrodes.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text:
In summary, a novel Cu electrode, HE-Cu, was prepared by electrochemical derivation of the MOF, HKUST-1. The surface of HECu was extremely rough as a consequence of the coating of Cu nanosheets composed of numerous nanoparticle subunits. The prepared HE-Cu electrodes catalyzed formation of CO and HCOOH as well as the selective formation of C2H4 and C2H6 as the gaseous products during electrochemical CO2R. Due to the unique surface structure of HE-Cu, CO2 adsorption and ESCA were greatly enhanced. Stepped Cu (211) surfaces, edge sites and (200) facets are considered as active sites for CO2R on HE-Cu determined by various physio-chemical and electrochemical characterizations. The large number of exposed Cu edge sites, together with higher ESCA and greater CO2 adsorption of HE-Cu, greatly enhanced CO2R activity and inhibited the HER. The selectivity for HCOOH generation onHECu was enhanced with the help of stepped Cu (211) surfaces, while the increased selectivity for C2 products was promoted by both stepped Cu (211) surfaces and (200) facets. In addition, production of CH4 was totally suppressed as a consequence of the edge sites and (200) facets. Our results suggest that electrochemical reduction of a MOF can provide a promising electrode with high CO2R activity and C2 product selectivity.
